cells.html:
An astronomical object can be a star, a galaxy or a quasar. A galaxy can be elliptical, spiral or irregular. A star can have the spectral type O, B, A, F, G, K or M, each with distinct physical properties. A single probability cannot describe three or more classes, as it does for two. We need one set of probabilities that adds up to 1 for each object.

A simple idea is to apply binary classification several times and compare each class with all the others. This idea has a flaw, because the separate classifiers can contradict each other. The remedy is to model all classes at once, with a softmax function that generalizes the sigmoid function. Maximum likelihood then gives a loss for \(K\) classes, which generalizes the binary cross-entropy.

We first show why binary decisions fail and how one-hot vectors represent the class labels. We then derive the softmax function and the cross-entropy loss. Information theory explains what the cross-entropy loss measures, through entropy and mutual information. Astronomers also use these measures to choose observations that best distinguish between competing models. We then derive the gradient and train the model with stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We end with practical points such as numerical stability and initialization.

8.1 Multi-Class Classification vs. Binary Classification

We want a model for many classes whose predictions do not contradict each other.

One-vs-Rest Limitations

In the One-vs-Rest strategy, we train one binary classifier for each class \(C_k\). Each classifier separates class \(C_k\) from “not \(C_k\)”, which combines all other classes.

This approach can lead to logical inconsistencies. Take three classes \(C_1\), \(C_2\) and \(C_3\). We train one classifier that separates \(C_1\) from the rest and another that separates \(C_2\) from the rest. These two already show the inconsistency. A classifier claims a point when it predicts its own class, and a point goes to \(C_3\) when neither classifier claims it. Each classifier has its own linear decision boundary, and the two boundaries, which cross, divide the feature space into four regions, as Figure 8.1 shows.

In the region that both classifiers claim, the \(C_1\) classifier predicts \(C_1\) and the \(C_2\) classifier predicts \(C_2\). Both predictions can have high confidence. The point cannot belong to two classes at once. Each classifier is trained on its own question, so their answers can disagree.

One-vs-One Limitations

The One-vs-One strategy avoids the combined group “not \(C_k\)”. It trains a separate binary classifier for each pair of classes, so \(K\) classes need \(K(K-1)/2\) classifiers. Three classes need three classifiers, which compare \(C_1\) with \(C_2\), \(C_2\) with \(C_3\) and \(C_1\) with \(C_3\). It still produces contradictions.

The classifiers decide independently, so their decisions can form a circular contradiction. Imagine three experts who each compare only two classes. For one point, the first expert ranks \(C_2\) above \(C_1\), the second ranks \(C_3\) above \(C_2\), and the third ranks \(C_1\) above \(C_3\). The rankings form a loop without a winner, as Figure 8.2 shows. Pairwise votes in an election can form the same loop, which is known as a voting paradox.

In the contradictory regions, the classifiers give no single answer. In practice, the label in such a region reflects the implementation and says little about patterns in the data. A multi-class classifier must therefore treat all classes simultaneously. Galaxy morphology, stellar type identification and exoplanet categorization need predictions without contradictions.

8.2 One-Hot Encoding for Multi-Class Problems

The first step is to rethink how we represent the class labels. A binary problem needs only one scalar label, usually 0 or 1, but this representation breaks down for more than two classes.

A first idea from binary classification is to use consecutive integers. Galaxies could be 0 for elliptical, 1 for spiral and 2 for irregular, and stars 0 for O and 1 for B.

Integer labels impose an artificial order on the classes. The sequence 0, 1, 2 suggests that spiral galaxies lie between elliptical and irregular galaxies, although the classes have no such order. In the binary case, we take 1 minus the prediction probability to swap the classes. For several classes, a new numbering changes the predictions of a model that treats the integers as numbers.

We need an encoding that suggests no order. One-hot encoding does this with one vector for each class.

A one-hot vector has \(K\) entries, one for each class. We put a 1 in the position of the class and 0 in all other positions. Class 1 (for example elliptical galaxies) becomes \([1, 0, 0, \ldots, 0]\), class 2 (spirals) becomes \([0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0]\), and class 3 (irregulars) becomes \([0, 0, 1, \ldots, 0]\).

One-hot encoding treats the classes symmetrically. Each class is a unit vector along a different coordinate axis. Geometrically, the classes are corners of a \(K\)-dimensional hypercube, which generalizes the square and the cube. Each pair has the same Euclidean distance \(\sqrt{2}\).

One-hot encoding also appears outside astronomy. A language model that predicts the next word of a text solves a multi-class problem. Its classes are the words of a vocabulary of tens or hundreds of thousands of words, and each word is a one-hot vector. At each position of the text, the model predicts a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The softmax function and the cross-entropy loss of this chapter also train such a model.

8.3 Multi-Class Logistic Regression

The training labels are one-hot vectors, so the model must output a vector as well. It predicts one probability for each class at the same time. This model is also called multinomial logistic regression or softmax regression.

The model outputs a probability vector \(\mathbf{p} = [p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_K]\), where \(p_k\) is the probability of belonging to class \(k\). Each \(p_k\) must lie between 0 and 1, and the probabilities must sum to 1, \(\sum_{k=1}^K p_k = 1\).

In the galaxy example, the training label of an elliptical galaxy is the one-hot vector \([1,0,0]\), while the model might output \(\mathbf{p} = [0.70, 0.25, 0.05]\). This vector means 70% elliptical, 25% spiral and 5% irregular. The model must map features to such probability vectors and respect their constraints.

A probability vector shows how confident a classification is, and in astronomy the confidence varies with data quality. A bright, well-resolved galaxy might receive \([0.95, 0.04, 0.01]\), a confident elliptical. A faint or poorly resolved galaxy might receive \([0.45, 0.40, 0.15]\), which means that the model is uncertain between elliptical and spiral. A galaxy with both spiral and irregular features might receive \([0.10, 0.45, 0.45]\), which means that the model cannot tell spiral from irregular. Such equal probabilities can also describe a galaxy that is truly intermediate between the two types.

In binary classification, a linear function cannot model a probability directly, because probabilities are bounded and linear functions are not. The logit transformation maps the bounded probability to the unbounded log-odds, which is the logarithm of the ratio of the two class probabilities. We therefore model the log-odds by the linear function \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}\), with a constant 1 appended to \(\mathbf{x}\) for the bias.

With \(K\) classes, we must transform the probability vector \(\mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x})\) so that a linear function can model it. The transformation must treat all classes together.

The idea is to compare all classes with one reference class, as the binary case compares class 1 with class 0. Probabilities sum to 1, so \(K\) classes have only \(K-1\) degrees of freedom, and each probability can be expressed relative to one reference class. Any class can be the reference, like the choice of an origin in a coordinate system.

We construct \(K-1\) probability ratios by comparing each class \(C_k\) with the reference class, which we label class \(K\). It plays the role of class \(C_0\) in Chapter 7. Bayes’ theorem gives \[ \frac{P(C_k|\mathbf{x})}{P(C_K|\mathbf{x})} = \frac{p(\mathbf{x}|C_k)P(C_k)}{p(\mathbf{x}|C_K)P(C_K)} \text{ for } k = 1, ..., K-1. \]

As in the binary case, the logarithm of each ratio can take any real value, so a linear function can model it. We model each log-ratio as \[ \ln\left(\frac{P(C_k|\mathbf{x})}{P(C_K|\mathbf{x})}\right) = \mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}. \]This gives \(K-1\) weight vectors \(\mathbf{w}_k\), one for each non-reference class. We optimize them together, because the probability of each class depends on all of them, as the softmax function below shows. In the One-vs-Rest strategy, each classifier works alone. Adjusting \(\mathbf{w}_1\) changes the relation between class 1 and the reference class and, through it, the relation between class 1 and each other class.

In the galaxy example, the reference class is irregular galaxies. Adjusting the weights that separate elliptical galaxies from it also changes how the model separates elliptical from spiral galaxies. No binary classifier for that pair is needed. The decision boundaries therefore depend on one shared set of weight vectors. The shared weights make the boundaries fit together, which independent binary classifiers cannot guarantee.

We now convert the \(K-1\) unbounded log-ratios back into \(K\) probabilities.

8.4 The Softmax Function

In the binary case, the sigmoid function is the inverse of the logit. It gives the probability of class 1 from the log-odds \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}\) \[ P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x})}. \] The reference class receives the remaining probability, \(P(C_0|\mathbf{x}) = 1 - P(C_1|\mathbf{x})\).

For \(K\) classes, we need an analogous function that turns the \(K-1\) linear predictions into \(K\) valid probabilities. This generalization of the sigmoid function is the softmax function, and we derive it as in the binary case.

We solve for the individual probabilities. Exponentiating the log-ratio model gives \[ \frac{P(C_k|\mathbf{x})}{P(C_K|\mathbf{x})} = \exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}) \text{ for } k = 1, \ldots, K-1, \] and therefore \[ P(C_k|\mathbf{x}) = P(C_K|\mathbf{x})\exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}) \text{ for } k = 1, \ldots, K-1. \]

The probabilities satisfy \[ \sum_{k=1}^K P(C_k|\mathbf{x}) = 1. \] We substitute the expression for \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x})\) in the terms with \(k < K\). Factoring out \(P(C_K|\mathbf{x})\) then gives\[ P(C_K|\mathbf{x})\left(1 + \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x})\right) = 1. \] Solving for the reference class gives \[ P(C_K|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{K-1} \exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x})}, \] and each other class \(k \neq K\) then has the probability \[ P(C_k|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x})}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{K-1} \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x})}. \]

A more compact form uses a weight vector \(\mathbf{w}_K = \mathbf{0}\) for the reference class. This vector is fixed, so we do not optimize it. It gives \(\exp(\mathbf{w}_K^T\mathbf{x}) = 1\), and the denominator \(1 + \sum_{j=1}^{K-1} \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x})\) equals \(\sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x})\). The reference class then has the same form as all other classes.

The probability of each class \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, K\) is therefore \[ P(C_k|\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x})}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x})}. \]This function turns \(K\) linear predictors into a probability distribution over \(K\) classes, and it is called the softmax function. Only the \(K-1\) vectors \(\mathbf{w}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{w}_{K-1}\) are free parameters.

The softmax function does not change when we subtract the same vector \(\mathbf{v}\) from all \(K\) weight vectors. The factor \(\exp(-\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{x})\) appears in the numerator and the denominator and cancels. Choosing class \(m\) as the reference means \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{w}_m\). The weight vectors become \(\mathbf{w}_k - \mathbf{w}_m\) and describe the same probabilities. For maximum likelihood without a weight penalty, the predictions therefore do not depend on the reference class.

The binary case is the special case \(K = 2\). With \(\mathbf{w}_2 = \mathbf{0}\) for the reference class, the softmax function gives \[\begin{aligned} P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) &= \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_1^T \mathbf{x})}{\exp(\mathbf{w}_1^T \mathbf{x}) + 1} \\ &= \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\mathbf{w}_1^T \mathbf{x})}. \end{aligned}\]This is the sigmoid function of binary classification. The reference class receives the remaining probability \(1 - P(C_1|\mathbf{x}) = 1/(1 + \exp(\mathbf{w}_1^T\mathbf{x}))\).

Decision Boundaries

The model divides the feature space into regions for the different classes. A boundary between two regions is a place where the model is equally uncertain between two classes. Classes \(j\) and \(k\) are equally likely where \[ P(C_j|\mathbf{x}) = P(C_k|\mathbf{x}). \]

The probabilities share the same denominator, so equal probabilities require equal numerators, \(\exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x}) = \exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T\mathbf{x})\). Taking logarithms gives \[ \mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}. \]This equation defines a hyperplane in feature space where classes \(j\) and \(k\) are equally likely. A hyperplane generalizes a line in two dimensions and a plane in three dimensions (Section 7.4). For \(K\) classes there are \(\binom{K}{2}\) such hyperplanes, one for each pair of classes. Here \(\binom{K}{2}\) means \(K\) choose 2, the number of pairs that we can pick from \(K\) classes, and it equals \(K(K-1)/2\).

Each hyperplane divides the space into a region where class \(j\) is more likely, \(\mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x} > \mathbf{w}_k^T\mathbf{x}\), and a region where class \(k\) is more likely, \(\mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x} < \mathbf{w}_k^T\mathbf{x}\). The feature entries of \(\mathbf{w}_j - \mathbf{w}_k\) are normal to the hyperplane, so they set its orientation. The bias entry sets its position. The difference of the two linear predictors changes fastest along this normal.

This resembles the One-vs-One strategy, but here all pairs come from one probability distribution. The decision boundaries are the parts of the hyperplanes where the two equally likely classes are more probable than all other classes.

To find the predicted class at a point, we take \[ \text{argmax}_k P(C_k|\mathbf{x}). \] This operation returns the class with the highest probability. It gives a definite answer, but the probabilities also show the uncertainty. If two classes have similar probabilities, the model is uncertain between them, even though the argmax still picks one. The probabilities \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x})\) therefore tell us more than the boundaries do.

Suppose that one linear prediction \(\mathbf{w}_m^T\mathbf{x}\) is much larger than the others. Then \(\exp(\mathbf{w}_m^T\mathbf{x})\) dominates the denominator, so \(P(C_m|\mathbf{x})\) approaches 1 and all other probabilities approach 0. Choosing the class with the largest of the \(K\) linear predictions gives probability 1 to that class and 0 to the others. That choice jumps from one class to another where two predictions cross. The softmax function is a smooth and differentiable version of this choice of the maximum, which explains its name. When several linear predictions are similar, the softmax function spreads the probability over the corresponding classes.

In two dimensions, each hyperplane becomes a line, and three classes \(C_1\), \(C_2\) and \(C_3\) have three pairwise lines. Parts of these lines bound the regions in which one class has the highest probability. All probabilities come from one softmax function, so the regions cannot contradict each other as in One-vs-One. The probabilities add up to 1, so no region belongs to two classes or to no class, as in One-vs-Rest. The decision boundaries can form a pattern like a peace sign, as in Figure 8.3, or like the Mercedes-Benz logo. Three regions radiate from a central point where all three lines meet.

Four classes give six pairwise lines, as \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\). They can form a pattern like a window pane, as in Figure 8.4, but some pairs of classes share no border. In this example, \(C_1\) and \(C_4\) are such a pair, because \(C_2\) or \(C_3\) is more probable wherever \(C_1\) and \(C_4\) have equal probability. Each point still has one probability distribution over all classes from the softmax function.

8.5 Multi-Class Cross-Entropy Loss

To find the set of all \(K-1\) weight vectors \(\{\mathbf{w}_k\}_{k=1}^{K-1}\), we use maximum likelihood as in the binary case. We choose the weights that make the observed data most probable under the model.

The Bernoulli distribution of the binary case has two outcomes, and now each example has \(K\) possible outcomes. The distribution over \(K\) classes is called the categorical distribution. Let \(\mathbf{t}\) be the one-hot label of an example, with \(t_k = 1\) if the example belongs to class \(k\) and 0 otherwise. For one example, the likelihood is the probability of its observed label given the model \[ L = \prod_{k=1}^K P(C_k|\mathbf{x}, \{\mathbf{w}_k\}_{k=1}^{K-1})^{t_k}. \]The factor of a class with \(t_k = 0\) equals 1, and only the factor of the true class differs from 1. For an object of class 2, \(t_2 = 1\) and all other \(t_k = 0\), so the likelihood is \(P(C_2|\mathbf{x}, \{\mathbf{w}_k\}_{k=1}^{K-1})\).

For \(N\) independent examples, the joint likelihood is the product of the individual likelihoods \[ L = \prod_{i=1}^N \prod_{k=1}^K P(C_k|\mathbf{x}_i, \{\mathbf{w}_k\}_{k=1}^{K-1})^{t_{ik}}. \] Here \(i\) indexes the \(N\) examples and \(k\) the \(K\) classes, and \(t_{ik}\) is the \((i,k)\) element of the one-hot label matrix. We take the logarithm, which avoids numerical underflow, and change its sign so that we minimize. We also divide by \(N\), so that the scale does not depend on the data set size. The result is the loss \(E\) \[ E(\{\mathbf{w}_k\}_{k=1}^{K-1}) = -\frac{1}{N} \ln L = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K t_{ik} \ln P(C_k|\mathbf{x}_i, \{\mathbf{w}_k\}_{k=1}^{K-1}). \]

For \(K = 2\), the multi-class cross-entropy reads \[\begin{aligned} E &= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^2 t_{ik} \ln P(C_k|\mathbf{x}_i, \{\mathbf{w}_k\}_{k=1}^{1}) \\ &= -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[t_{i1} \ln \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_1^T \mathbf{x}_i)}{1 + \exp(\mathbf{w}_1^T \mathbf{x}_i)} + t_{i2} \ln \frac{1}{1 + \exp(\mathbf{w}_1^T \mathbf{x}_i)}\right]. \end{aligned}\] Each example belongs to one class, so \(t_{i1} + t_{i2} = 1\). We write \(t_i = t_{i1}\) and \(t_{i2} = 1 - t_i\), and the loss becomes \[ E = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N [t_i \ln y_i + (1-t_i)\ln(1-y_i)], \] where \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}_1\) and \(y_i = \exp(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i)/(1 + \exp(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))\) is the predicted probability of class 1. The probability of class 2 is \(1 - y_i = 1/(1 + \exp(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{x}_i))\). This is the binary cross-entropy loss of Chapter 7.

For \(K\) classes, we write the predicted probability from the softmax function as \(y_{ik}\) \[ y_{ik} = P(C_k|\mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x}_i)}, \] where \(\mathbf{w}_K = \mathbf{0}\) for the reference class. The loss is then \[ E = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K t_{ik} \ln y_{ik}. \]

8.6 Information Theory and Cross-Entropy

In the previous section we derived the loss \(E\) from maximum likelihood. It is called the cross-entropy loss, and information theory explains this name. A good classifier works as a compression of the data. With good weights the model predicts the class from the features, so the true class of an object can be sent in a shorter message.

We first define the mutual information. We then link it to the loss through the entropy.

Mutual Information

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with values in the sets \(\mathcal{X}\) and \(\mathcal{Y}\). Their mutual information \(I(X;Y)\) measures how much knowing one of them tells us about the other \[ I(X;Y) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} P(X=x,Y=y) \log_2\left[\frac{P(X=x,Y=y)}{P(X=x)P(Y=y)}\right]. \]

The ratio \(P(X,Y)/(P(X)P(Y))\) compares the joint probability with the product of the marginal probabilities, which is the joint probability for independent variables. For independent variables the ratio is 1, and its logarithm is 0. For dependent variables, the ratio is larger than 1 where the two variables occur together more often than independence predicts. The logarithm turns the multiplicative comparison into an additive one. The logarithm has base 2, and the example below explains its unit.

Mutual Information Versus Correlation

From Chapter 3, the Pearson correlation coefficient is \[ \rho_{XY} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y} = \frac{\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]}{\sigma_X \sigma_Y}. \] Here \(\mathbb{E}\) denotes the expectation, \(\mu_X\) and \(\mu_Y\) are the means, and \(\sigma_X\) and \(\sigma_Y\) are the standard deviations. The correlation coefficient detects only linear trends.

Consider points that lie close to a circle centered at the origin. Despite the clear pattern, the correlation coefficient is near zero, because moving right sometimes increases \(Y\) and sometimes decreases it, which cancels in the average. Knowing \(X\) still limits \(Y\) to two values near \(\pm\sqrt{1-X^2}\) on the unit circle. Mutual information is positive here, because the joint distribution \(p(x,y) = P(X=x,Y=y)\) differs from the product of the marginals \(p(x)p(y)\). It detects any relationship in which knowing one variable tells us about the other, whatever its shape. Figure 8.5 compares the two measures.

An Example and the Bit

As an example, let \(Y\) be a number drawn uniformly from 1 to 16. Let \(X\) tell us whether \(Y\) lies in the first half (1 to 8) or the second half (9 to 16). Then \(P(Y=y) = 1/16\) for each \(y\) and \(P(X=\text{first}) = P(X=\text{second}) = 1/2\). Given \(X\), we have \(P(Y|X=\text{first}) = 1/8\) for \(y\) from 1 to 8 and 0 otherwise, and \(P(Y|X=\text{second}) = 1/8\) for \(y\) from 9 to 16 and 0 otherwise.

Rewriting the ratio inside the logarithm gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{P(X,Y)}{P(X)P(Y)} &= \frac{P(Y|X)}{P(Y)}. \end{aligned}\]This ratio compares the probability of \(Y\) after we know \(X\) with the probability before. Where \(P(Y|X) > P(Y)\), the logarithm is positive and we gain information. The mutual information is \[\begin{aligned} I(X;Y) &= \sum_{x,y} P(X,Y) \log_2\left[\frac{P(Y|X)}{P(Y)}\right] \\ &= 16 \cdot \frac{1}{16} \log_2\left[\frac{1/8}{1/16}\right] \\ &= \log_2(2) = 1 \text{ bit}. \end{aligned}\]

The ratio \((1/8)/(1/16) = 2\) means that knowing \(X\) halves the number of possible values of \(Y\). One bit is the information of a yes or no answer that halves the number of equally likely values. It is also one binary digit, 0 or 1, of a code. The base 2 of the logarithm gives the result in bits, so \(X\) provides one bit of information. We still need three more bits to find which of the remaining eight values is correct, and \(X\) provides only the first bit. The mutual information therefore counts, on average, the yes or no questions that knowing one variable saves when we specify the other.

The factor \(P(X,Y)\) in the sum averages this information gain over all combinations of \(X\) and \(Y\) according to their joint distribution. Only 16 of the 32 combinations occur, and each has probability \(1/16\), so the average is the same one bit.

Mutual Information in Classification

In classification, \(X\) stands for the input features of a galaxy, such as its concentration index or its asymmetry. The class \(\mathit{C}\), for example elliptical, spiral or irregular, takes the place of \(Y\). The mutual information \(I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\) then measures how much the features tell us about the class.

We rewrite the mutual information with conditional probabilities \[ I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C}) = \sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}} p(\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}) \ln\left[\frac{p(\mathit{C}|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathit{C})}\right]. \]

Here \(p(\mathit{C}|\mathbf{x})\) is the probability of class \(\mathit{C}\) given the features \(\mathbf{x}\). In our classifier, the softmax function computes it as \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x})\). From here on we replace \(p(\mathit{C}|\mathbf{x})\) by the model probability, and we take \(p(\mathbf{x},\mathit{C})\) and \(p(\mathit{C})\) from the training data. Then \(I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\) is the information that the model has about the class. The base of the logarithm sets the unit, which is bits for base 2 and nats for base \(e\). The loss uses base \(e\), so we write \(\ln\) below and \(\log_2\) when we count bits.

Entropy

Entropy measures uncertainty. A code writes each value as a string of bits, and a message is a sequence of such strings. The entropy is the smallest average number of bits per value that a code can reach, when the logarithm has base 2. For a variable \(\mathit{C}\) with distribution \(p(\mathit{C})\), the entropy in nats is \[ H(\mathit{C}) = -\sum_\mathit{C} p(\mathit{C}) \ln p(\mathit{C}). \] Dividing by \(\ln 2\) gives the entropy in bits.

Imagine that we encode the galaxy types of a catalog. If elliptical, spiral and irregular galaxies appear with equal frequency, then \(p(\mathit{C}) = 1/3\) for each type, and with the base-2 logarithm \[ H(\mathit{C}) = -3 \cdot \frac{1}{3} \log_2 \frac{1}{3} = \log_2 3 \approx 1.58 \text{ bits}. \]We therefore need at least 1.58 bits per galaxy on average, which we approach when we code many galaxies together. A code with equal length for all types needs 2 bits, and the codes 0, 10 and 11 already average 1.67 bits. In these codes no string is the beginning of another string, so a reader can split a message into types without separators.

Entropy is smallest when one class dominates, because most objects then belong to the same class and few bits suffice on average. It is largest when the classes are balanced, because no class is more likely than the others. If the types have unequal frequencies, short codes for common types and long codes for rare types lower the average length. In English text, the letter e is much more common than z, so e gets a shorter code than z. If spiral galaxies are more common than irregular galaxies, for example, the entropy falls below 1.58 bits.

Cross-Entropy as Code Length

The cross-entropy loss averaged over \(N\) training examples is \[ E(\{\mathbf{w}_k\}) = -\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{t_{ik}}{N} \ln P(C_k|\mathbf{x}_i). \] The term \(t_{ik}/N\) is the weight that example \(i\) gives to class \(k\) in the empirical distribution of the training data. This distribution gives each training example the probability \(1/N\) (Section 3.7). The sum over examples is therefore an expectation over the empirical joint distribution \(p(\mathbf{x},\mathit{C})\) of the training data. Written as a sum over pairs of features and classes, the same loss reads \[ E(\{\mathbf{w}_k\}) = -\sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}} p(\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}) \ln p(\mathit{C}|\mathbf{x}). \]

This loss is called a cross-entropy. To see why, imagine that we send the true class of each object to a receiver who already knows the features. The receiver can use our model probabilities to design an ideal code, and a class with probability \(q\) then needs \(-\log_2 q\) bits. The average length of these messages is the cross-entropy loss, in bits when the logarithm has base 2. A better model gives shorter messages, which saves bits compared with a code that ignores the features. The code lengths \(-\ln p(\mathit{C}|\mathbf{x})\) come from the model and the average comes from the data, which gives the name cross-entropy.

Loss, Entropy and Mutual Information

Expanding the mutual information gives \[\begin{aligned} I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C}) &= \sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}} p(\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}) \ln p(\mathit{C}|\mathbf{x}) - \sum_{\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}} p(\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}) \ln p(\mathit{C}) \\ &= -E(\{\mathbf{w}_k\}) - \sum_{\mathit{C}} p(\mathit{C}) \ln p(\mathit{C}). \end{aligned}\] The first sum is \(-E\), as the sum over pairs of features and classes above shows. In the second sum, \(\sum_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x},\mathit{C}) = p(\mathit{C})\), so the second term is the entropy \(H(\mathit{C})\) defined above. It depends only on the class frequencies of the data set. The loss is therefore the entropy minus the information that the model has about the class \[ E(\{\mathbf{w}_k\}) = H(\mathit{C}) - I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C}). \]

In coding terms, \(H(\mathit{C})\) is the average length of the best code that ignores the features. The code built from the model probabilities has average length \(E\), so \(I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\) is the saving. Because the entropy does not depend on the model parameters, minimizing the cross-entropy loss maximizes the information that the model has about the class.

Divide the training examples into groups with the same features. The best code for a group uses the fractions of its examples in each class, and no model code is shorter on average. The loss of any model is therefore at least the average uncertainty about the class that remains given the features. This quantity is the conditional entropy \(H(\mathit{C}|\mathbf{x})\), the entropy of the class within a group, averaged over the examples. Subtracting it from \(H(\mathit{C})\) gives the mutual information of the training data, which we write \(I_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\).

The information \(I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\) that the model has about the class is therefore at most \(I_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\). The two are equal when the model probabilities equal the fractions of the training examples in each class for the same features. In training, we find the combination of input features that gives the model the most information about the class.

Feature combinations that work well for classification have high mutual information with the class labels. The concentration index measures how concentrated the light of a galaxy is toward its center. It is such a feature for galaxy classification, because it tells us a lot about the morphological class. A feature such as the absolute sky position typically has low mutual information with morphology.

The entropy term bounds the information about the class that the model can learn. For a perfect prediction, \(P(C_k|\mathbf{x}_i) = 1\) whenever \(t_{ik} = 1\), so the model probabilities equal the one-hot labels and the loss is \(E = 0\). Then \(H(\mathit{C}) = I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\), which means the model has extracted all the information that the features hold about the class. Optimizing the cross-entropy therefore brings \(I(\mathbf{x};\mathit{C})\) as close as possible to \(H(\mathit{C})\). The remaining gap equals the loss, which is the uncertainty about the class that the model leaves.

In our classifier, the entropy term comes from the empirical class distribution of the training data and equals \[ H(\mathit{C}) = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{N_k}{N} \ln \frac{N_k}{N}. \] Here \(N_k\) is the number of examples of class \(k\) among the \(N\) examples. Neither better features nor better weights can change this term.

When the loss approaches zero, a receiver who knows the features needs almost no extra bits to recover the class. A large loss suggests room for improvement, either in the choice of features or in how we combine them. If the classes overlap in feature space, however, this model keeps a loss above zero, because the features do not determine the class.

8.7 Gradient Descent for Multi-Class Classification

To minimize the loss with gradient descent, we need its gradient with respect to each weight vector \(\mathbf{w}_j\) for \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, K-1\). This is harder than in the binary case. A change of one weight vector changes the probabilities of all classes through the normalization term of the softmax function.

The loss is convex in the weights, as in the binary case of Chapter 7. For an example whose true class is \(c\), the loss term is \(-\ln y_{ic} = -\mathbf{w}_c^T\mathbf{x}_i + \ln\sum_{l=1}^K \exp(\mathbf{w}_l^T\mathbf{x}_i)\). This is a linear function of the weights plus a log-sum-exp function of linear functions of the weights. The log-sum-exp function is the logarithm of a sum of exponentials, and it is a standard convex function. Sums of convex functions are convex, and the loss averages such terms over the examples. A minimum that gradient descent finds is therefore a global minimum.

Deriving the Gradient

By the chain rule, the gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{w}_j\) is \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K t_{ik} \frac{\partial \ln y_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j}. \] We must find how a change of \(\mathbf{w}_j\) affects each \(y_{ik}\). There are two cases, the probability \(y_{ij}\) of class \(j\) itself and the probabilities \(y_{ik}\) of the other classes \(k \neq j\).

We start with the derivatives of \(y_{ik}\) with respect to the logit \(z_{ij} = \mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x}_i\). The logit is the linear prediction of class \(j\) before the softmax function, and for two classes it is the log-odds of Chapter 7. The reference class has \(z_{iK} = 0\). For \(k = j\), both the numerator and the denominator of \(y_{ij} = e^{z_{ij}}/\sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}}\) depend on \(z_{ij}\). The derivative of the denominator is \(e^{z_{ij}}\), because only its term \(l = j\) depends on \(z_{ij}\). The quotient rule \((f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g^2\) with \(f = e^{z_{ij}}\) and \(g = \sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}}\) gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial y_{ij}}{\partial z_{ij}} &= \frac{e^{z_{ij}} \cdot \sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}} - e^{z_{ij}} \cdot e^{z_{ij}}}{(\sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}})^2} \\ &= \frac{e^{z_{ij}}}{\sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}}} \cdot \frac{\sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}} - e^{z_{ij}}}{\sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}}} \\ &= y_{ij} \cdot (1 - y_{ij}). \end{aligned}\]

For \(k \neq j\), only the denominator of \(y_{ik}\) depends on \(z_{ij}\), and we get \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial y_{ik}}{\partial z_{ij}} &= \frac{\partial}{\partial z_{ij}} \frac{e^{z_{ik}}}{\sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}}} \\ &= e^{z_{ik}} \cdot \frac{-e^{z_{ij}}}{(\sum_{l=1}^{K} e^{z_{il}})^2} \\ &= -y_{ik} \cdot y_{ij}. \end{aligned}\] Now we need \(\partial \ln y_{ik}/\partial \mathbf{w}_j\). The probability \(y_{ik}\) depends on the logits \(z_{il}\) of the \(K-1\) free classes, so the chain rule gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln y_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} &= \sum_{l=1}^{K-1} \frac{\partial \ln y_{ik}}{\partial z_{il}} \cdot \frac{\partial z_{il}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j}. \end{aligned}\]Only one term of this sum is nonzero, because \(\partial z_{il}/\partial \mathbf{w}_j = \mathbf{x}_i\) for \(l = j\) and 0 for \(l \neq j\). The sum therefore reduces to \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln y_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} &= \frac{\partial \ln y_{ik}}{\partial z_{ij}} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i. \end{aligned}\]

For \(k = j\), we insert \(\partial y_{ij}/\partial z_{ij} = y_{ij}(1-y_{ij})\) and get \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln y_{ij}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} &= \frac{1}{y_{ij}} \cdot \frac{\partial y_{ij}}{\partial z_{ij}} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i \\ &= (1 - y_{ij}) \cdot \mathbf{x}_i. \end{aligned}\]

For \(k \neq j\), we insert \(\partial y_{ik}/\partial z_{ij} = -y_{ik}\,y_{ij}\) and get \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln y_{ik}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} &= \frac{1}{y_{ik}} \cdot \frac{\partial y_{ik}}{\partial z_{ij}} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i \\ &= -y_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i. \end{aligned}\]

Substituting these results into the gradient gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} &= -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ t_{ij} \cdot (1 - y_{ij}) \cdot \mathbf{x}_i - \sum_{k \neq j} t_{ik} \cdot y_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i \right]. \end{aligned}\]The factors \(y_{ij}\) and \(\mathbf{x}_i\) do not depend on \(k\), so they come out of the sum over \(k \neq j\). The label vector is one-hot, so \(\sum_{k=1}^K t_{ik} = 1\) and \(\sum_{k \neq j} t_{ik} = 1 - t_{ij}\). Therefore \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} &= -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ t_{ij} - t_{ij} \cdot y_{ij} - y_{ij} \cdot (1 - t_{ij}) \right] \mathbf{x}_i \\ &= -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ t_{ij} - t_{ij} \cdot y_{ij} - y_{ij} + t_{ij} \cdot y_{ij} \right] \mathbf{x}_i \\ &= -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (t_{ij} - y_{ij}) \mathbf{x}_i. \end{aligned}\]

The gradient for each weight vector is therefore \[ \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (y_{ij} - t_{ij}) \mathbf{x}_i. \]Each example contributes the difference between the predicted probability \(y_{ij}\) and the true label \(t_{ij}\) of class \(j\), scaled by \(\mathbf{x}_i\). This has the same form as in the binary case, but now we update \(K-1\) weight vectors, one for each non-reference class.

In binary classification, a misclassified example moves one decision boundary in one direction. In multi-class classification, a single misclassified example moves several weight vectors at once. Some weight vectors move toward the features of the example and some away from them, in a coordinated way.

Consider a galaxy of true class \(j \neq K\) that receives a high probability for another class \(k \neq K\). For the true class, \(y_{ij} - t_{ij} = y_{ij} - 1\) is negative, because \(y_{ij} < 1\). The update multiplies the gradient by \(-\eta\), where \(\eta\) is the learning rate, so it adds a positive multiple of \(\mathbf{x}_i\) to \(\mathbf{w}_j\). This moves \(\mathbf{w}_j\) toward the features of the galaxy. For the wrong class \(k\), \(y_{ik} - t_{ik} = y_{ik} > 0\), so the update subtracts a multiple of \(\mathbf{x}_i\) from \(\mathbf{w}_k\).

The size of the corrections depends on how the probability is distributed over the classes. As in binary classification, high-confidence mistakes cause the largest corrections. If \(y_{ij} \approx 0\) for the true class, the update \(|y_{ij} - 1| \approx 1\) is at its maximum. If the missing probability belongs to one wrong class \(k \neq K\) with \(y_{ik} \approx 1\), then \(|y_{ik} - 0| \approx 1\) as well, and both weight vectors receive large updates. If the probability is spread over many wrong classes with small \(y_{ik}\), each update is smaller, although their sum remains large. The reference class receives no update, because \(\mathbf{w}_K\) is fixed.

Extending SGD to Multi-Class Problems

SGD works as in the binary case. We approximate the full gradient with a mini-batch of \(M\) examples and update the parameters iteratively.

For \(K\) classes, the update rule is \[ \mathbf{w}_j^{(\tau+1)} = \mathbf{w}_j^{(\tau)} - \eta \cdot \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^M (y_{ij}^{(\tau)} - t_{ij})\mathbf{x}_i \quad \text{for } j = 1, 2, \ldots, K-1, \]where \(\tau\) counts the iterations. We update the \(K-1\) weight vectors together.

Most techniques of the binary case carry over with little change, such as mini-batches, learning rate schedules, adaptive learning rates and regularization. Adaptive learning rates set a separate step size for each parameter (Section 15.3). Weight decay with strength \(\lambda\) adds the penalty \(\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{K-1}\|\mathbf{w}_j\|^2\) to the loss. It adds the term \(2\lambda\mathbf{w}_j\) to the gradient of each weight vector, as in Chapter 7.

8.8 Implementation Considerations

Numerical Stability

The softmax function uses exponentials, which can overflow or underflow. The multi-class case computes \(K-1\) exponentials of free logits where the binary case computes one, and a single large logit \(\mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x}_i\) can overflow the sum.

A standard remedy subtracts the largest logit before the exponentiation \[ y_{ik} = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}_i - \max_j \mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x}_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x}_i - \max_j \mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x}_i)}. \]This leaves the probabilities unchanged, because the factor \(\exp(-\max_j \mathbf{w}_j^T\mathbf{x}_i)\) appears in the numerator and the denominator and cancels. The largest exponent is now 0, so the exponentials are at most 1 and the denominator is at least 1.

Parameter Initialization

We initialize each free weight vector with small values, for example samples from a normal or a uniform distribution. Both distributions are easy to sample in any dimension, also for the many features of astronomical data. Small values keep the logits near zero, so all classes start with probabilities near \(1/K\).

Random values are common, because weight vectors that start equal and receive equal gradients would stay equal. This model does not need them. In general, the different labels give each weight vector a different gradient, so even zero initial values work. The loss is convex, so training reaches the same minimum loss from any initial values, for a suitable learning rate. This holds when the loss has a minimum at finite weights. It has no minimum when a hyperplane separates one class from the others, because the loss then keeps falling as the weights grow (Chapter 7).

The initialization changes only the speed and the path of the optimization. Random restarts, which train several models from different starting points and keep the best one on a validation set, are therefore unnecessary for this model.

Matrix Formulation for Efficiency

For an efficient implementation, we organize the weight vectors as the rows of a matrix \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times D}\). Here \(D\) is the feature dimension including the constant 1 for the bias, and the last row \(\mathbf{w}_K\) is fixed to zero. This allows vectorized computation, which replaces loops by matrix operations, for all classes and examples at once.

The data matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\) holds \(N\) examples with \(D\) features each. The product \(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}\) gives all logits \(z_{ij}\) of all examples in one operation, and the last column is zero, \(z_{iK} = 0\), because \(\mathbf{w}_K = \mathbf{0}\). We apply the softmax function to each row of \(\mathbf{Z}\), after subtracting the largest logit of the row for numerical stability. This gives all class probabilities \(y_{ik}\).

The matrix form suits mini-batches. For a mini-batch \(\mathbf{X}_{\text{batch}} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times D}\), the logits are \(\mathbf{Z}_{\text{batch}} = \mathbf{X}_{\text{batch}}\mathbf{W}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times K}\). Linear algebra libraries are optimized for such operations and run them in parallel, which can be orders of magnitude faster than loops.

The gradient also takes a matrix form. Let \(\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}\) contain the predicted probabilities and \(\mathbf{T} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}\) the one-hot labels. Then \[ \nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{1:K-1}} E = \frac{1}{N}(\mathbf{Y}_{1:K-1} - \mathbf{T}_{1:K-1})^T \mathbf{X}, \] where \(\mathbf{W}_{1:K-1}\) denotes the first \(K-1\) rows of \(\mathbf{W}\), and \(\mathbf{Y}_{1:K-1}\) and \(\mathbf{T}_{1:K-1}\) denote the first \(K-1\) columns of \(\mathbf{Y}\) and \(\mathbf{T}\). The rows of this gradient matrix are the gradients \(\partial E/\partial \mathbf{w}_j\) for \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, K-1\).

We fitted the weights by maximum likelihood, which gives one set of weights and one probability for each class. The probabilities describe how confident the model is for these weights, but they do not say how uncertain the weights are. Chapter 9 treats this second uncertainty with Bayesian methods for binary logistic regression. The non-Gaussian likelihood of the sigmoid function needs techniques beyond those of regression.

8.9 Tutorial: Classifying Strong Lensing Images

This tutorial applies the softmax function and the cross-entropy loss of this chapter to objects in deep images from the James Webb Space Telescope. It sorts them into classes, so that strong lensing arcs can be found among them. The full tutorial can be found at https://tingyuansen.github.io/statml/ as tutorial 8.

A massive galaxy or galaxy cluster is a lens that deflects the light of galaxies behind it, as general relativity predicts. When a background galaxy lies almost behind the lens, it appears as a stretched arc or as several images. Such a strong lens can magnify early-universe galaxies, and the arcs of a cluster measure its mass, mostly dark matter. A survey has too many objects to check by eye, so a classifier can sort them.

In Section 7.10 one probability separated two classes of stars. The objects in deep images form many classes of look-alikes, such as arcs and blurry diffuse ones (Figure 8.6a). One probability is not enough for three or more classes, and separate One-vs-Rest classifiers can claim an object twice or leave it unclaimed (Section 8.1). One model must therefore treat the classes together. The softmax function turns one linear prediction for each class into probabilities that add up to one (Section 8.4).

The probabilities need features and targets. A large pre-trained model supplies the features of each object (Section 15.9), and one-hot labels name the true class without an order (Section 8.2). Maximum likelihood then gives the cross-entropy loss, which is small when the true class has a high probability (Section 8.5). Gradient descent minimizes it and so raises that probability, and confident mistakes change the weights most (Section 8.7).

We check the classifier on test objects, since it is meant for unlabeled ones. The largest probability usually lies on the true class, as for most of the nine objects in Figure 8.6b. When the model errs, the true class usually has the second largest probability. A survey can add the probabilities of the arc classes and check the objects with a high sum.

Further Reading

Dietterich and Bakiri (1991, 1995) developed error-correcting output codes, which give each class a code word of binary classifier outputs. Allwein et al. (2000) unified the One-vs-Rest and One-vs-One reductions to binary classifiers. Fürnkranz (2002) analyzed round robin classification, with one classifier for each pair of classes. Luce (1959) proposed a model of choice probabilities that leads to the softmax function. McFadden (1974) connected it to choice models in economics and to multinomial logistic regression, and Theil (1969) extended the logit model. Bridle (1990) named the softmax function. Dennis and Schnabel (1983) developed numerical methods for unconstrained optimization. Polyak and Juditsky (1992) showed that averaging the parameter values of successive steps speeds up stochastic gradient methods.
